opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the fact that, for a lot of people, quantum computing gets presented as this sort of magic wand. You hear that a quantum computer would just try every possible answer in parallel and then pick out the right one, and that would let you solve any hard problem instantly. If that were true, it would be amazing, but it's not how quantum mechanics works. And understanding *why* it's not how it works turns out to be one of the most interesting things you can study.

The key point is that quantum mechanics isn't about probabilities; it's about these things called amplitudes, which can be positive or negative or even complex numbers. The whole trick of a quantum algorithm is to choreograph things so that, for each wrong answer, the contributions to its amplitude interfere destructively and cancel out, while for the right answer they reinforce each other. Nature only lets you do that for problems with very special structure. Factoring is one, thanks to Peter Shor, and simulating quantum physics itself is another. But for something like the NP-complete problems, the traveling salesman or satisfiability, we have good reason to believe that quantum computers would give you at most a modest speedup, like the square-root speedup from Grover's algorithm, not an exponential one.

So for me, studying the limitations is really a way of understanding what quantum mechanics is actually telling us about the nature of computation and, ultimately, about the physical world. If you could build a device that solved NP-complete problems efficiently, I'd almost take that as evidence that our understanding of physics was wrong somewhere. These limits are almost like a new kind of physical principle, analogous to the second law of thermodynamics or the impossibility of faster-than-light signaling.

And there's a practical side too. There's been an enormous amount of hype in this field, with companies and journalists making claims that quantum computers will revolutionize optimization, machine learning, finance, you name it. Part of my job, as I see it, is to be the person who says: okay, but what's the actual evidence for a speedup here? Knowing where the limits are is what lets us separate the real, genuinely exciting applications from the wishful thinking.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what quantum computers could not efficiently do, including NP-complete problems, and frames a device capable of solving them as hypothetical (“If you could build a device…”).

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the thing people often find strange is that I've spent most of my career on the question of what quantum computers can't do, rather than what they can. And I think that's actually where a lot of the intellectual action is.

Here's the way I'd put it. When quantum computing first got popular in the '90s, after Shor's algorithm, there was this enormous temptation to say, "Okay, quantum computers try all possible answers in parallel, so they'll just solve everything." And that's wrong. It's wrong in a very specific and interesting way. A quantum computer doesn't just explore every branch and hand you the one you want. You get a superposition, and when you measure it you see one outcome, chosen at random. The entire game is to choreograph interference so that the paths leading to wrong answers cancel each other out and the paths leading to the right answer reinforce. And it turns out that for most problems, nobody knows how to arrange that, and there are good reasons to believe you often can't.

So the limitations question is really the question of what's special about the problems where quantum computers do help. Factoring has this beautiful periodic structure that Shor was able to exploit. For something like an unstructured search problem, Grover's algorithm gives you a square-root speedup, and we can prove that's the best you can do in that setting. That's a limitation result, but to me it's one of the most illuminating facts in the field, because it tells you quantum mechanics isn't magic. It's a specific resource with specific rules.

And honestly, the other reason I got into this is that if you want to understand what a new model of computation can do, you have to understand what it can't do. Otherwise you don't understand it at all. Classical complexity theory taught us that. P versus NP, these are questions about limits, and they shaped how we think about everything. I wanted to ask the same kinds of questions about quantum computers, both because I thought the answers would be deep, and because I didn't want the field drowned in hype. If we're going to build these machines, and we are, we should be honest about what they're for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what quantum computers can and cannot do, and says these machines are still being built. It does not clearly frame the inquiry as studying what a computer we do not yet have would be unable to do.

astra-6.text:
What interests me is that quantum computing forces us to ask what the laws of physics actually allow us to compute. A quantum computer isn’t just a faster version of an ordinary computer. It gives us a different set of resources, and the fascinating question is where those resources help and where they don’t.

People sometimes describe a quantum computer as trying every possible answer simultaneously. But if you measure a superposition, you only get one outcome. The hard part is arranging interference so that wrong answers cancel out and useful answers become more likely. That works spectacularly for some problems, but we don’t know how to make it work for everything.

So studying limitations is really about understanding the source of the power. Can quantum computers solve NP-complete problems efficiently? We don’t know, but we have substantial reasons to be skeptical. And figuring out why is just as intellectually interesting to me as finding a new quantum algorithm. It helps us distinguish what’s genuinely possible from what we merely wish were possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what quantum computers may be unable to do, including efficiently solving NP-complete problems, but does not communicate that the subject is a computer we do not yet have.

sol-6.1.text:
What fascinates me is that quantum computers force us to ask where the limits of computation actually come from. Are they features of the machines we happen to build, or are they woven into the laws of physics?

Quantum computing gives us dramatic examples of how changing the physics changes what we can compute efficiently. But it doesn’t appear to make every hard problem easy. And understanding that boundary is, to me, just as interesting as finding a new quantum algorithm.

For example, people often hear that a quantum computer tries every possible answer simultaneously. But if you measure it, you only get one outcome. The challenge is to arrange interference so that the wrong answers cancel and the right answer becomes likely. Understanding when you can do that—and when you can’t—is really the heart of the subject.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of quantum computers and notes they do not make every hard problem easy, but it does not frame this as investigating what a not-yet-existing computer would be unable to do.
